name: OCL-MLA
reason: No numeric comparison anywhere reachable. The repo (about 10 stars, 147 commits, Los Alamos National Security copyright 2012) has a README (file name README, no extension) that only describes logical 'performance' and 'auxiliary' devices, hash-based kernel registration, the autoconf build and matching C and Fortran 90 examples. The doc/ directory holds only Makefile.am and doxygen.conf.in, with no benchmark or timing numbers and no comparison against raw OpenCL. The listed project page tuxfan.github.io/ocl-mla is on a blocked host (*.github.io) and was not opened. It is also a thin wrapper that adds convenience, not speed, so no faster-than claim is plausible.

name: oclkit
reason: No numeric comparison against any named baseline. The README (GPL v3, about 17 stars, last commit 2017-04-18) only shows sample output of its own diagnostic binaries: check-infrastructure-times (clCreateContext 0.150983 s, clBuildProgram 0.002060 s), check-launch-latencies (22.12 us wall clock on a GeForce GTX TITAN Black, 16.33 us on a GTX 580) and a 1000 ns profiling timer resolution. These are device or runtime measurements, not a comparison with raw OpenCL or another wrapper, and the README says nothing about being faster. examples/ holds more check-* programs (queue impact, concurrent queues, PCI bandwidth) that compare OpenCL queue configurations with each other, not against another library, and ship no committed results.

name: offbrand
listed_description: Collection of generic, reference-counted data structures (C, MIT).
reason: No numeric comparison or speed claim reachable. The repo (MIT, about 81 stars, last commit 2025-05-13 'Update README.md') has a three-sentence README (reference-counted generic data structures in C plus bash scripts for class creation and testing), and directories apps (minlog, pfinder), docs, include, scripts and src with no benchmark directory. The documentation site theck01.github.io is on a blocked host (*.github.io) and was not opened, but the repo carries no performance statement that it could back.

name: OMath
listed_description: Cross-platform modern general purpose math library written in C++23 that suitable for cheat/game development. ZLIB.
reason: Repo not reachable: github.com/orange-cpp/omath, github.com/orange-cpp and raw.githubusercontent.com README.md paths on HEAD, main, master and dev all return HTTP 404 in this session (the owner page is 404 too, so the repo was probably removed, renamed or made private). Web search snippets only repeat the tagline ('blazingly fast', 'optimized for performance using AVX2', constexpr heavy) with no numbers and no named baseline (GLM, Eigen, DirectXMath), and a follow-up search for an omath benchmark found nothing. A Gitea mirror (identichosting.duckdns.org) is blocked. Directional claim only, nothing verifiable.

name: Onigmo
listed_description: Fork of Oniguruma, supporting more advanced regexps. BSD-2-Clause.
reason: No numeric comparison reachable for Onigmo itself. README, doc/ (API, FAQ, RE, UnicodeProps.txt) and the 4-page wiki (Home, branches_and_tags, how_to_debug, incompat) contain no benchmark or speed claim; it focuses on Perl 5.10+ syntax (\K, \R, conditionals) and Ruby 2.0+ compatibility. Issue titles on performance (#100 'performance regression if quantifier lower bound is 1', #97 'Performance problem with /k/i and /s/i', #151 add API to mitigate ReDoS) have no PCRE comparison numbers. The only shootout found with PCRE2 numbers, rust-leipzig/regex-performance, measures upstream kkos/oniguruma master and not Onigmo (recorded under Oniguruma); Onigmo's engine is a fork of Oniguruma 5.9.x with different code, so those rows are not transferable. Last commit 2024-06-15, 679 stars, BSD-2-Clause.

name: Open MPI
reason: No first-party numeric comparison against a named baseline reachable. The repo (2.7k stars, BSD) README and docs (history.rst, index.rst, tuning-apps) only state a goal of 'extremely high, competitive performance' with no numbers; www.open-mpi.org (papers page) and laro.lanl.gov (IPDPS 2006 'Infiniband scalability in Open MPI', snippet said latency up to 10% better than MVAPICH) are EGRESS_BLOCKED, so that paper could not be opened. Third-party results found are mixed and not claims of being faster: open-mpi/ompi issue #11765 (MPI_Allgatherv of 40 million ints per process, Open MPI 5.0.x with UCX) shows Open MPI 5.153137 s vs Cray MPICH 0.724109 s on 32 nodes (about 7x slower) and only 4.941182 s vs 7.161596 s on a single node, closed as not planned; pmodels/mpich issue #7188 reports MPICH slower than Open MPI in a GPU ping-pong but gives graphs and no numbers. Open MPI is the incumbent others compare against, so no record.
